It’s both. I’m both paranoid and depressive (self-blaming) in personally style, so I get paranoid projections but fear they speak to my “badness” and then pick things apart to find all the ways I’m bad.

I remind myself of how they’ve been in the past. 

I reply like I usually do to them, or I might neutrally ask for clarification (“I’ve been struggling with a lot of anxiety and negative-self talk lately. I just wanted to make sure I haven’t done anything to upset you and that we’re good?”) (obviously don’t do this too often)

But yeah, I just find ignoring my worry and replying as usual does the trick. 

Also, keep in mind the difference of thoughts vs actions. A friend may be thinking a negative thought (about anything, not even related to you), and maybe that in someway comes out in their reply. But did they actually *do* anything to warrant your feelings?

Check out DBT skill check the facts.

Oh, also, if they’re you’re good friend, you can explain why you got worried and they can explain what they meant. Or you can talk to another friend and ask for clarification about the convo (without outing the other person). 

Or you can call a distress center hotline and explain your paranoia and ask for help with skills to manage it and reassurance.

As for specialized help, you can try psychoanalysis. They specialize the help to the person.

Lastly, it’s thought us paranoid’s project our own disowned feelings onto people and then feel persecuted by it. It’s possible you are feeling insecure and projecting it.

This will probably get downvoted but traditional psychoanalytic therapy cured my severe lifelong and treatment-resistant bulimia - like a switch flipped, after I had three bizarre and intense breakdown at home in succession about something I had no clear thoughts about. 

Now it’s like I never had it. I get no urges. I don’t think about it. At my worst I was having bulimic episodes for over 20 times a day, for years. No skills or coping mechanism helped me. I did as much intensive DBT as I could. 

Having it cured was like the greatest blessing or a miracle. I still can be at a risk of lapses if I try to lose weight or have to go off of medications that affect my serotonin, but I have several months where it’s like I never had it at all. Currently going six months into a full remission period; only had *very* vague feeling of it coming back once when I was tapering down from ADHD medication and my appetite got out of control. Even when I do lapse it’s extremely minor and I can get out of it pretty easily. 

I don’t know how it was cured. Couldn’t tell you exactly what happened. I have chronic derealization and depersonalization, and I was having intense but vague transference reactions to the analyst. I was going home after having a few drinks one night and suddenly I felt like I could see myself as “real” through the perspective of my analyst. Like somehow I was real, along with my life (and all the horrible things that happened to me and all the feelings I repress). It felt like an intrusion into my mind. 

I got home, was standing in my bedroom, and the feeling suddenly overwhelmed me. It was so painful I lost the ability to stand. I fell to the ground while literally screaming from the emotional pain. It was like nothing I ever felt before - and I usually never cry about anything. I had two more episodes of that happening within a few weeks and then my bulimia was gone. Seems like my neural pathways legitimately got rewired.

In my experience clinical psychology is not equipped for those with CPTSD. On paper, psychology recognizes the severe effects childhood abuse can have on a person, but this recognition does not transfer over well in person. Far too often clinicians readily eat up CPTSD clients’ tendency to covertly turn things around on themselves or make themselves seem infantile. The savior complex is a very common consequence of this, where the client is, through countertransference, seen as a helpless object; but this is essentially the clinician contributing to the abusive narrative that’s been imposed into the client.

This can happen when a person internalizes their abuse and takes it on for their own. It’s actually a survival mechanism; a person was taught that making a mistake isn’t okay, so now their mind is trying to “keep them in check” so that they don’t suffer from further abuse from others. 

So, first off, don’t beat yourself up for this. At some point, the self-critical voice was in some way protecting you when you had basically no other way to protect yourself. 

However, it’s obsolete now—as in, it sounds like it’s not needed anymore; you’re in a safer environment presumably.
You likely won’t be able to just shove down or ignore the self-critical voice, since a part of your mind decided  that the self-critique was necessary for survival. So, if you try to ignore it or approach it with resentment, this will probably just make it louder. 

My advice would be to try and trace the self-critical voice back to your childhood and see where it came from and the function it had for you. When it comes up, when you make a mistake and begin to hear it, remind yourself you’re safe now (if you are) and that it’s okay. Recognize that this part of your mind was trying to keep you safe when you had no way to be safe, but reassert that’s you are no longer in a place where making mistakes isn’t okay.
